books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Constitution of the State of California, Article I, Section 18 (1849)

stimulus.source_note: Constitution of the State of California, Article I, Section 18, adopted at Monterey, 1849. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Neither slavery, nor involuntary servitude, unless for the punishment of crimes, shall ever be tolerated in this State.

[Original summary: California's convention wrote this constitution at Monterey in the fall of 1849, after gold drew tens of thousands of settlers to the territory in a single year. The convention asked Congress to admit California as a free state.]

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The gold rush and California's statehood application are best understood together as showing that

options.text: a rush of settlers forced Congress to face the slavery question early.
the federal government planned California's settlement to keep slavery out of the West.
options.misconception: The settlement was a rush of individual gold seekers, not a federal plan; the constitution was written by Californians at Monterey, not by Washington.

options.text: Californians wrote their constitution mainly to please Southern senators.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Southern senators opposed admitting California free, since it would tip the Senate; the convention wrote its constitution for Californians, not to please the South.

options.text: gold mining made slavery profitable in California, so voters protected it.
options.misconception: The constitution banned slavery in California, so voters did not protect it. Background from the books: the gold rush was driven by free prospectors seeking their own fortunes, and the convention wrote a free-state constitution.

rationales.A: Gold drew tens of thousands to California in a single year, and the convention asked Congress to admit the state free. Background from the books: Congress had spent years avoiding the slavery question, and the sudden application forced it onto the floor.
rationales.B: The settlement was a rush of individual gold seekers, not a federal plan; the constitution was written by Californians at Monterey, not by Washington.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Southern senators opposed admitting California free, since it would tip the Senate; the convention wrote its constitution for Californians, not to please the South.
rationales.D: The constitution banned slavery in California, so voters did not protect it. Background from the books: the gold rush was driven by free prospectors seeking their own fortunes, and the convention wrote a free-state constitution.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the rush: gold pulled tens of thousands west in a single year, faster than any plan could manage.
2. Follow the rush to its result: a convention at Monterey, a constitution banning slavery, and an application for statehood.
3. Background from the books: Congress had dodged the slavery question for years, and now a finished fact from the far West demanded an answer.
Remember: settlement can outrun politics; when people move faster than Congress, Congress has to catch up.
